paragraphs.text: William was at the aquarium watching a scuba diver swim among the fish. The diver scattered food into the water as the fish gathered around her.
"Cool!" William thought, heading to the next exhibit.
A sign on an empty eel tank read: "I'll be back after my checkup with the veterinarian!"

Finally he came to his favorite exhibit. A long tentacle explored the glass. A round, black eye looked at him. Did the octopus recognize him? William knew octopuses were smart. He had read they could open jars and use tools.
"You must like octopuses. I see you here often," said a woman. "I'm Dr. Blackwell. I'm the marine biologist who takes care of this guy."
"I love octopuses!" said William. "I'm saving for a pet octopus."
"Sea animals need special care—especially an octopus" said Dr. Blackwell. "Do you want to see how I take care of our octopus?"
"Yes!"
"Let's go."

Dr. Blackwell led William to a room with big water tanks and pumps. "These pumps are connected to all of the tanks. They can move thousands of liters of water per minute. The equipment in this room keeps the tanks clean with filters. We also treat the water to kill algae and bacteria. In the next room is the heating and cooling system. Tropical fish need warm water."
"I have a heater for my aquarium at home," said William.
"Our giant Pacific octopus needs cooled water."
William frowned. He had never heard of an aquarium cooler.
Next they went into a huge kitchen where chefs were chopping fish and seaweed.
"This kitchen is held to a higher standard than restaurant kitchens," explained Dr. Blackwell. "To keep our animals healthy, we feed them food similar to what they eat in the wild."
She pointed to a plastic container marked Giant Pacific Octopus. "Our octopus eats shrimp and squid."
"Uh-oh," William thought. That sounded expensive.
Dr. Blackwell handed William a book. "Every animal has special needs. These are instructions for caring for an octopus."
"It's over a hundred pages!"

"Marine biologists study the habitat of each animal. We have to know the right size for each animal's tank. Those instructions also tell us which animals can live together. Clownfish, for example, can live with many other types of fish and sea anemones."
"But the octopus lives alone," said William.
"Right. Octopuses will fight and eat their neighbors."
William read from the book. "Octopuses need a den and don't like bright light."
"They can be mischievous too. One octopus squirted water at the light over its tank—and broke it!" She raised her eyebrows. "What will you do if your pet octopus inks his tank?"
William sighed. "I guess octopuses are difficult pets."
"You can always come visit our octopus," Dr. Blackwell said.
"Thanks, Dr. Blackwell!"
As William left, he put some money in the donation box for the aquarium. Now he felt like the aquarium octopus was his octopus too.

2.title: The Tallest Animal in the World

paragraphs.text: Do you know what animal is the tallest in the world? You guessed it! It's the giraffe! Follow me and let's take a close-up look at these marvelous creatures.
Here we see a group of giraffes. As you can see, giraffes are the tallest animals in the world. The male giraffe can grow to 5.5 meters. The female giraffe is usually a little bit shorter.
What makes these animals so unusual? It's their very, very, very long necks, of course.

Actually, this neck makes it possible for the giraffe to reach very high. It can reach the soft and tender leaves on the tops of trees. As you can see, there aren't many trees around here. So the giraffe's long neck helps it find food to stay alive.

Can you see that giraffe over there? Look at how the giraffe must spread its legs very wide. It's the only way it can get its head down low. Why is that? The giraffe's neck is very long, but it is not very flexible.
In fact, the giraffe's neck has only seven vertebrae. We humans have seven vertebrae too. But look how short our necks are! With such big bones, the giraffe's neck cannot bend very well.

The giraffe's neck is not the only unusual thing about this animal! The giraffe has a tongue that can stretch to almost 45 centimeters long. Also, its head can stretch almost in a straight line. So, the giraffe can reach the highest leaves. In fact, a giraffe eats about 34 kilograms of leaves a day!
The giraffe doesn't drink often─maybe once every two or three days. It gets water from the soft leaves!
You know, the giraffe's body is not very big. In fact, the giraffe's body is about the size of a horse's body. But it's the legs and the neck that make it the tallest animal in the world!

The legs of a giraffe are very strong! The body of a giraffe is designed to support the head. See the large muscles at the top of its legs? Those muscles are powerful. A lion that attacks a giraffe will quickly learn that from a kick!
Even though the giraffe has such a long neck, its voice box is very small. Giraffes aren't able to make loud noises. We usually don't hear them making any noises at all.

Then how do they protect themselves? Well, you know how they can kick! Also, the giraffe's ears are very sensitive. So is its nose. In fact, a giraffe will often smell danger and use its very long legs to run away quickly!
Its best protection is its color. It's hard to see a giraffe because it looks like it's a part of a tree.
Giraffes don't sleep more than thirty minutes a day. Sometimes you'll see a giraffe lying down for a short time to rest, but many times they rest with their eyes open!
Well, I hope you enjoyed your close-up view of the giraffe. Aren't they amazing? The next time you see a giraffe, remember: there's much more to this unusual animal than just its long neck!
Hi, everyone! My name is Bobby and I'm a bird. I live on the back of a hippopotamus—a male hippopotamus, actually. His name is Henry.
Henry and I live near a lake in Africa. Hippos live near rivers and lakes all over Africa. But they don't live on any other continent.
How did a tiny bird and a big hippo become friends? Well, we help each other out!
I eat ticks and bugs off Henry's body. In return, he lets me live on his back.
Hippos help other animals too. There are many plants around the rivers, swamps, and lakes. Henry makes a path through the thick plants. Then other animals can walk to the water.
Henry also helps plants. Henry poops in the water, but it's okay. The plants grow strong from the nutrients in his poop. Other animals eat the plants and get strong.

As you know, it gets extremely hot in Africa. Do you wear suntan lotion to protect your skin from the bright sun? Believe it or not, Henry makes his own suntan lotion! He sweats red oil. The oil prevents his skin from cracking or burning. I like to put some on my beak when I am hot!
In ancient Greece, people thought hippos sweated blood. But I know it is just skin oil.
Henry spends most of the day in the water. It's cooler there, and Henry's skin is especially suited to water. But Henry isn't a very good swimmer. He usually walks on the river or lake floor.
Hippos' eyes, nostrils, and ears are on the tops of their heads. This helps them breathe and watch for danger when they are in the water.
Henry can also stay underwater for five minutes. He closes his nostrils and presses his ears against his head. That way, water does not get in.
When Henry comes out of the water, he makes funny snorts and hisses.

It's hot now, but soon it will be evening. In the evening Henry and I leave the lake. Food is the reason Henry leaves the water. His appetite is huge! He can eat 35 to 45 kilograms of grass for dinner.
Uh-oh! "Henry, are you going underwater again? I want to stay here longer!"
When Henry goes underwater, I have to find a new place to rest. I would never argue with a hippo!
Talk with you later. Good-bye!

A long time ago, many beavers lived in Scotland. But their fur became very popular for making coats, and people thought beavers tasted delicious. They hunted all the beavers until they were gone. That happened over four hundred years ago.

Today scientists are worried that the beavers have not returned. So they have decided to learn more about the beaver’s habitat. Habitat means the natural place where an animal lives. If scientists know more about how beavers live, they can encourage beavers to return to Scotland.

When a beaver turns three years old, it leaves its family and swims downriver to build a new home. A beaver’s home is called a lodge. It looks like a big pile of sticks, but it is actually a carefully designed house.
Beaver lodges are made of small tree branches and mud that are piled in the shape of an upside down bowl. Most lodges are two to three meters high, three to six meters wide, and full of tunnels.

Some tunnels lead to the rooms inside where the beavers live. Other tunnels store food. There are also secret tunnels that confuse predators—so hungry animals don’t make beaver soup for dinner! Beavers build their lodges in streams, and the entrance is always underwater so that it is hard to find.

For a long time, scientists were confused about the size of a beaver lodge. Most beaver families have a mom, a dad, and one to four babies, which are called kits. Why did they need so much room? After watching beavers for a long time, scientists found two answers to their question.

First, beavers build big homes because they need thick walls to keep out predators. Second, beavers need a place to store their food. Since beavers do not hibernate, they need a warm, safe place and lots of food when the weather gets cold. In the north many lakes turn to ice in the winter. The ice often traps beavers inside their lodge, so beavers need to store enough food to make sure they don’t get hungry.

Beavers will often build their lodge with young trees on the inside so they can eat the bark during winter. Beavers love to eat bark, especially from aspen and cottonwood trees. Beavers also like to eat clover and raspberry bushes, but their favorite food is water lilies. Many people think beavers eat fish, but this is not true.

The best way to find a beaver habitat is to look for a lot of water. Beavers always build a dam near their lodge. It makes the stream slow down and creates a pond. This way the lodge is surrounded by water, making it look like a tiny island.

After watching beavers for a long time, scientists learned that beavers live for about ten years. Once two beavers decide to make a family, they never leave each other. Beavers somehow always know when there are too many beavers living on their river. They have the right-sized family to keep the river from getting crowded.
Now that the scientists know what beavers like to eat, where they like to live, and how they build their homes, they are working to make Scotland a place that beavers can call home.

One day some scientists looked around and saw that the rivers were very dirty, and that there were less fish to catch. They also noticed that there were fewer birds and dragonflies, and that the trees were starting to die. They couldn’t find what was causing the problem. But they noticed something else was missing—the beaver. So scientists decided to study how beavers live so that they can bring them back to the rivers.

Wherever beavers live, they make big changes to nature. In fact, the only creatures who affect nature more are humans! However, unlike humans, the changes that beavers make are good for the other animals and plants around them.

Once a beaver finds an empty spot on a stream or river, it builds a dam. As soon as the dam is built, the land upstream begins to fill with water. The extra water changes the land behind the dam into a wetland. A wetland is a wide area of mud and water, and wetlands are very important habitats. In fact, over half of North America’s endangered species need wetlands to survive.

Once a beaver makes its dam, it takes care to make sure the water level around the dam stays high. The beaver does this to protect its home, but it also protects nature. The dam slows down a river, which helps make the water cleaner. And instead of the river carrying good soil away to the ocean, the dam keeps the soil in the forest.

Even though beavers cut down trees to make their dams, they actually help the trees to grow. A beaver’s favorite trees for eating and building are cottonwoods and aspens. Both of these trees make hundreds of baby trees every year. However, if all the baby trees lived, they would eventually get too crowded, and they all would die. But when the beaver takes out some of the trees, it gives the rest more room to grow. This helps keep the forests healthy.

Beavers eat only plants, and this makes its other animal friends happy. The wetland created by a beaver dam gives otter, mink, muskrats, deer, bears, dragonflies, turtles, frogs, and ducks—and lots of other birds—a place to grow and hunt. The reason scientists couldn’t find fish or dragonflies or birds is that the beavers weren’t there building their dams.

Even though beavers keep the rivers clean, the trees growing, and the other animals alive, many people get angry with beavers. When dams make wetlands, sometimes they ruin a farmer’s field or flood a road. Some dams make it hard for fish to travel in streams. But when people try to trap beavers to take them away, a new beaver always moves in. So scientists are studying ways to help beavers and humans live together so we can all make changes that will be good for nature.

Beavers once lived all over Europe and North America. But because they have beautiful fur, people hunted them to make warm coats. As beavers started to disappear, scientists became worried and decided to learn more about them.

The first thing scientists studied was a beaver’s body. Beavers are part of the rodent family, which means squirrels and rats are their cousins. Their front teeth are very long, and beavers use them to cut wood and pull off bark. Like a hamster or rat, a beaver’s teeth grow and grow and grow for its whole life! However, beavers are bigger than all of their cousins. Most beavers weigh fifteen to thirty-one kilograms, and are almost 117 centimeters long!

Even though beavers have fur, they like to be in water instead of on land. Beavers are very beautiful swimmers, but they look silly when they try to walk. Their heavy tails make walking very difficult.

A beaver tail is the size of a computer keyboard, and it helps a beaver stand, balance heavy logs, and steer in the water. And, if an enemy comes too close, one beaver will warn other beavers by slapping its tail on the water.

When a beaver dives into the water, two important changes happen. First, it closes its eyes, nose, and mouth. Beavers have two kinds of eyelids: the inside one is clear—like goggles—and the outside one is black. When a beaver is underwater, it protects its eyes by using the goggle-like eyelids to see where it’s swimming. The beaver’s nose also has special skin inside which closes to keep out water.

However, its mouth is even more amazing. A beaver needs its front teeth to grab logs underwater, but it doesn’t want a mouthful of water and logs. Amazingly, its lips are behind its front teeth so that it can keep water out and still grab whatever it needs.

The second underwater change is when the beaver goes from a walker to a swimmer. On land, a beaver’s back feet look like its cousin's. But when it dives into water, the toes pull apart to show a web in between. This webbing helps it swim through water quickly.

Most beavers stay underwater for three to five minutes. But some can stay down for as long as fifteen minutes. That’s a long time for only one breath—especially since most humans stay underwater for less than sixty seconds.

Scientists were very impressed with the beaver’s body. Few animals can live in water and on land as well as the beaver. But scientists are still worried. The more that people wear fur coats, the fewer beavers there are in the wild. And the fewer beavers there are in the wild, the more problems scientists see in nature.
Now that scientists have learned about a beaver’s body, they know more about how a beaver lives. But scientists are still looking for ways to help beavers and humans live together.
My name is Kenny and I'm a koala. I'm native to Australia, which means that I'm originally from there. I eat, sleep, and live in the eucalyptus forests of Australia.

I eat only the leaves of the eucalyptus trees. I can eat up to five hundred grams of leaves a night. At night, you ask? Yes, at night. I like to eat during the night and sleep during the day. I'm nocturnal.
I don't drink a lot of water. That's because I get all the water I need from the leaves. In some of the native Australian languages, koala means "no drink." That's how we got our name.

I sleep in the branches of the eucalyptus tree. After I eat, I pick out a nice big branch and sleep. I usually sleep twenty hours a day. I sleep a lot, don't I? The rest of the time, I eat and move around.

I like to live up in the branches of the eucalyptus trees. I have two thumbs on each paw and long, sharp claws that make it easy for me to climb up and down the tree trunks. I can also leap from branch to branch.
When I run out of leaves to eat, I climb down and run to another tree. I don't like to stay on the ground too long because of cars and dangerous predators like the dingo, an Australian wild dog.

I'm a type of animal called a marsupial. Other marsupials are the kangaroo, the Tasmanian devil, and the wombat. Marsupials are different from other mammals because, unlike most mammals, the baby is underdeveloped when it's born. It needs to finish developing in its mother's pouch.

You see, when a baby koala is born, it is very, very small─almost the size of a pink jelly bean. Although the baby is blind and deaf, it crawls its way into the mommy's pouch. The baby attaches itself to the mother's nipple to get food to grow big and healthy. A baby marsupial is called a joey. So, baby kangaroos are also called joeys.
First, the joey develops eyes, ears, and fur. At about five months, the joey's eyes open and it's able to peer out of the pouch.
When it is six months old, the joey gets too big for the pouch and can't fit inside. When that happens, the joey rides on the back of its mother.

A joey leaves its mother when it becomes one year old, or when it gets a little brother or sister. In my case, I enjoyed staying with my mommy until I was one. But I was also very excited to go off on my own.
I like to live by myself. I'm territorial, which means that I don't like other koalas coming too close to where I live. But if you're nice, you can visit me anytime.

Tammy: Hi everyone, I’m Tammy. I’d like to welcome all the ants that have hatched today. It’s our tradition here at the ant colony to meet with the queen on the first day after hatching. I’ll be leading you all to her.

On our way there, I’ll give you a tour of the different parts of the colony. As you all know, this room is called the Pupae Room. This is where all of you developed in your final stage of growth. You see, the stages are egg, larvae, pupae, and then adult.

That room over there is where the larvae are kept. This is where you become pupae. Everyone, say hello to Nancy, the nurse ant. It’s her job to take care of the larvae and make sure they become pupae.
Ants: Hi, Nancy.
Nancy: Hi, everyone. This room is temperature controlled so that the eggs will all be nice and warm before they hatch. Better get back to work. Bye guys.
Tammy: Everyone, say hi to Fiona, the forager ant. It’s her job to make sure we have lots to eat.
Fiona: That’s right, everyone. We leave the colony to find food and bring it back.
Ant: What kinds of food do you gather?
Fiona: For the most part, we gather seeds, sugar, fruit, and sometimes, if we’re lucky, we find another insect. I have to go back to work now. See you all later.
Tammy: Everyone, that’s Annie, the architect ant. She helps build our nest and makes it bigger.
Ants: Hi, Annie.
Annie: Hi, everyone. It’s my job to dig and make new rooms and tunnels, especially now that we have so many new ants.
Annie: Oh my, look at the time, I have to get back to work.
Tammy: Now, everyone, we’re going to go near an exit to the colony. Be very careful. This is Susan, the soldier ant. It’s her job to protect our colony from predators.
Ant: Wow. What weapons do you use?

Susan: First of all, we use our antennae to smell other ants and make sure that they are a part of our colony. If the smell isn’t right, we use our stings to attack. Other types of ants spray acid on the enemy. Excuse me, but I have to go back to work.
Tammy: Now we’ve come to the end of our tour. You will all get to meet the queen. Hello, Your Majesty. The new adults have come to pay their respects.
Queen: Welcome, my children! I see that you’re all grown and ready to work. Working is very important to the survival of our colony. We need soldiers, architects, nurses, foragers, and many more.
Ant: But, Your Majesty, what’s your job?
Queen: My job is to make lots and lots of eggs.
Ants: Wow.
Queen: I’d like to congratulate you on your new life here in the colony. Now, let’s get to work!
Meet Lucy. She is a beautiful caterpillar. One morning she saw Sally Spider.
"Hi, Sally! What are you doing today?" asked Lucy.
"I am spinning a web to catch some lunch. Do you want to spin a web with me?" Sally asked.
"Oh, I’d like to spin with you. But I think I have too many legs!" said Lucy.
"That’s true. I only have eight legs," said Sally. "But you have sixteen! Wow."
Lucy laughed and said, "Yeah, they help me hold on to branches better."
"I’ve got to keep spinning," said Sally. "See you later, Lucy!"
Lucy said good-bye. Then she met Anthony Ant. "Hi, Anthony! What are you doing today?" she asked.
"I’m carrying food back to my house. I will save it until winter," Anthony said.
Lucy was very impressed. "I save my food too. But I save it inside my body."
"That’s very smart!" Anthony said.
"Hi, Lucy!" said a bee, drinking from a daisy.
"Hi, Bert! What are you doing today?" Lucy asked.
"I’m collecting pollen to share with the queen bee. Do you want some?" Bert asked.
"No, thank you. I ate my lunch already. Look at these leaves! Aren’t they delicious?" asked Lucy.
"Uh, sure! But I’d rather eat honey. See you tomorrow, Lucy!" And Bert flew off to a flower far away.
Can you guess Lucy’s favorite hobby? That’s right, it’s eating! She needs to eat a lot of leaves because she stores her food in her body.
"I ate so many leaves today! Maybe I will go someplace quiet and take a nap," thought Lucy. "Oh, and sleeping upside down sounds comfortable. I’m sleepy." Lucy started to snore.

Lucy is sleepy because she is about to make a big change! After eating many leaves for many months, she will shed her caterpillar skin and form a hard shell called a chrysalis. Inside her chrysalis, she will sleep for a long time. Can you guess what happens next?
"Hey, Sally. Have you seen Lucy lately?" asked Anthony.
"No, Anthony. I haven’t seen Lucy for two weeks!" Sally said. "Bert, have you seen Lucy?"
"No, Sally. I haven’t seen her either." Bert was very worried.
"I think we should go look for her. Do you want to come with me?" Anthony asked.
"Yes!" said Bert and Sally. They flew and crawled after him.
"Look, Anthony! There are Lucy’s clothes!" cried Sally. She pointed at Lucy’s old skin.
Bert looked at Lucy’s hard shell. "Why, it must be an evil monster! I think it ate Lucy!" He knocked on the monster’s shell. "Excuse me. Open up. Did you eat my friend, Lucy? Hello?"
Suddenly the chrysalis opened. "Lucy?" asked all three friends, confused.
"You’re beautiful!" said Sally.
"Thanks. So you like my new wings?" said Lucy, smiling.
"I sure do!" said Bert. "Will you join me for some leaves and pollen?"
"Sorry, Bert, but I have to fly across the field and lay over a hundred eggs!" said Lucy. "For once I’m not hungry! All I want to do is fly!"
Lucy floated off into the distance, and her friends cheered. "Bye, Lucy! We’ll miss you!"
Mr. Ribbit, the science teacher, cleared his throat."Ribbit! Do you know how we became frogs?" he croaked.
The young frogs looked at each other. Mr. Ribbit held up two pictures. In one hand was a picture of a tadpole. In the other was a picture of a frog.
"Today we are going to learn about metamorphosis. Ribbit!" he said.
"Meta . . . what?" asked Freddy. "Metamorphosis," Mr. Ribbit repeated. "It is how we change from tadpoles into frogs.

In the spring male frogs attract female frogs by singing. The frog couple starts their family in the pond. Ribbit! The male frog fertilizes the eggs in the water. A few days later, the eggs begin to change."
"Do they become tadpoles?" asked Hetty.
"Ribbit! Yes. At this stage, the head is big and the tail is very long," explained Mr. Ribbit.
"Soon the eggs hatch and the tadpoles come out. Tadpoles, like fish, use gills to breathe."
"But Mr. Ribbit, we aren't fish, are we?" asked Lily.
"Of course not! We are amphibians. Who knows what that means?"
"Amphibians can live on land and in water," answered Boris.
"Right! But at first, tadpoles can only live in the water."
"What do tadpoles eat?" asked Freddy.
"Ribbit! As soon as they are born, tadpoles eat plants and algae. A few days later, they develop teeth. Then the tadpoles start to eat insects."

Mr. Ribbit continued, "Tadpoles use their tails to swim. They are very active at this age. Tadpoles swim around in a group called a school. Six to nine weeks after they are born, metamorphosis begins. Ribbit! The back legs begin to appear and the tadpoles use them for swimming. The body grows larger, and the head begins to take shape. Next, the front legs begin to grow."
"That looks like my brother!" Hetty laughed.
"Ribbit! It looks just like a small frog except for the long tail. The tadpole is almost a frog now," said Mr. Ribbit.

"During the last days of metamorphosis, the tail slowly disappears into the body. Remember the tadpoles' gills? Ribbit! They don't need them anymore. The gills are covered over by skin. So the little frogs learn to breathe with their lungs. Once the tail is gone, the little ones can climb onto land. Now the tadpole is completely transformed into a frog. In a few days, the new frogs can leave the pond. They can enjoy life both in the pond and on land. Metamorphosis takes about 12 to 16 weeks.

There are many different kinds of frogs. Some like to live in the water. Others spend all their time on the land. But we always have to return to the water to start our own families," concluded Mr. Ribbit.
"Wow! We are special in many ways!" Victor exclaimed.
"It's interesting to know how we got here," the young frogs croaked. "We are proud to be frogs! Ribbit!"
Mandy is an active young woman. She goes to school like other people her age. She is studying music.
But Mandy is special in one way. Everywhere she goes, her best friend Henry leads her. Mandy is blind and Henry is her guide dog. Mandy and Henry do everything together.
Not all dogs can become guide dogs. Guide dogs have to be smart. They also have to be faithful to their owners. German shepherds, golden retrievers, and Labradors like Henry make good guide dogs.

Guide dogs start their training at a very young age. About seven or eight weeks after a puppy is born, it moves in with a family. These families are called puppy raisers. They volunteer to raise the puppy for one year.
It is important for guide dogs to feel safe and to have lots of love. They must learn to get along with other people. They must learn to get along with other animals.
Henry's first family was the Martins. The Martins had two little girls. Their names were Anna and Mimi. They loved Henry very much.
At night, Henry slept with Anna and Mimi. It is important for guide dogs to sleep inside the house. The Martins took care of Henry and loved him as part of their family.

After one year, it was time for Henry to return to the school. Henry began his special training. He learned how to obey commands. "Sit!" "Come here!" He learned to wait for the traffic light to change.

Henry was almost ready to be a guide dog. First, he and Mandy received training together. Mandy learned to give Henry orders and how to take care of him. Henry learned to love and trust his new owner.
Mandy walked with Henry to her school. Then they walked back home. Before long, Henry knew how to get to school and back by himself.
Henry makes sure that Mandy is safe wherever she goes. Henry is happy to take care of Mandy. "Thanks, Henry."
Even at home, Mandy and Henry spend every moment together. Mandy likes to play the piano. And Henry likes to sing along!
Mandy does not feel less able because she is blind. She feels special because she has Henry. Not only is Henry her guide dog, he is her best friend.
George hated worms. He didn't like to touch them. He didn't even like to look at them.
"Yikes! It's a worm. I hate worms," screamed George.
"What? You hate me? Do you also hate those pretty flowers?" asked the earthworm.
"No, I like them," said George.
"Well, then, you must like me too. I help all of those grow," said the worm.
George had never seen a talking earthworm. But he still didn't like worms.

"I am a great digger. I dig holes that help air and water get into the ground," said the worm. "Plants need a lot of air and water to grow. Without me the plants could not grow," said the worm with pride.
But George still didn't like worms.
"I also make food for the plants," said the worm.
"Really? How?" asked George.
"I eat soil that is filled with small bits of plants and bacteria. They go through my body and out the other end," said the worm.
"Plants eat your poo?" asked George with a laugh.
"That's right! It is called fertilizer," said the worm.
"But you are so small. How can one little worm help?" asked George.
George did not know that the earthworm was not alone. Even in George's small garden, there were more than five hundred earthworms.
"All my friends work together to help your garden," said the worm. "So do you still hate me?"
In a shy voice, George said, "No, but you are very dirty and yucky."
"I'm not dirty. I am very clean. Feel me!" said the worm.
"Well, I don't know," George said quietly.
"Come on!"
George carefully touched the worm.
"See! I'm not so bad," said the worm.
"Actually, you are kind of soft," admitted George.
Now George was beginning to like the worm.
"But, Worm, you don't have any bones," said George.
"That's right! I don't have arms or legs. I don't need them," explained the worm.
"You don't need them? How do you move?" asked George.
"I have muscles that go all around my body. I use them to push through the ground. Watch!"
"It must take a long time for you to go anywhere," George said with a laugh.
"That's true. I am a very slow mover, but I like it here in your garden. So I don't want to go very far," said the worm.
"Well, I am glad you are in my garden. You are a great helper," said George with a smile.
"Remember, worms are your friends," said the worm.
"I will!" said George.
Sally: Dr. Smith, what is this?
Dr. Smith: That is a time machine, Sally. With this machine, we can go back in time.
Sally and TIM: Wow! Can we try it?
Dr. Smith: Of course! Where do you want to go?
Tim: I want to see the dinosaurs.
Dr. Smith: No problem. Let's go! Hop in, Tim! Hop in, Sally! Here we are, 65 million years ago.
Sally: Wow! It looks very different. Everything is so big.
Dr. Smith: Yes, many of the plants are very big.
Tim: Dr. Smith, I don't see the dinosaurs.
Dr. Smith: Look up.
Tim: Wow! It's huge and scary-looking. Will it eat me?
Dr. Smith: No, it won't eat you, Tim. It is a plant eater.
Tim: Whew! That's good.
Dr. Smith: Besides, it's only a baby. Look over there, that is its mother.
Sally and TIM: Wow! That dinosaur sure is big.
Dr. Smith: That is one of the biggest dinosaurs ever, Sally. It is called a Brontosaurus. It weighs more than 28 tons and is about 25 meters long.
Tim: I hope it doesn't step on me.
Dr. Smith: That would be very bad. Let's explore more! But be careful.
Sally: Look at that dinosaur. It is smaller than the other ones.
Dr. Smith: Yes, it is an Iguanodon. It's a plant eater too.
Tim: If it's a plant eater, it won't hurt me. Hello, Iguanodon. How are you today?
Dr. Smith: Tim, watch out!
Sally: That was close. It almost hit you with its tail.
Dr. Smith: Yes, the Iguanodon has a very powerful tail. It can use its tail when it is attacked.
Sally: It also uses it to hit small boys.
All: Ha-ha-ha!
Tim: Maybe we should leave it alone.
Dr. Smith: That's a good idea, Tim.
Sally: Ah! Look over there. Look at that dinosaur. It has a very large head. What's its name, Dr. Smith?
Dr. Smith: It's a Triceratops. Its head is very big and it has three horns.
Tim: Its horns look very sharp.
Dr. Smith: Yes, they are. You can see one horn on its nose and the other two above its eyes. It uses the horns to protect itself.
Tim: I hope it doesn't poke me.
Sally: There's a very interesting dinosaur. It's very big, but it has a very small mouth. I wonder how it eats.
Dr. Smith: That is a Stegosaurus. It's a plant eater too. You're right. It does have a very small mouth.
Tim: Look at its back. It's bumpy.
Dr. Smith: Those are called back plates, Tim. The Stegosaurus uses them for protection.
Sally: Dr. Smith, I think that all plant eaters have some way to protect themselves.
Dr. Smith: Yes, Sally, you're right.
Tim: Look over there. What's that?
Sally: It looks like a giant egg.
Dr. Smith: Oh, don't touch it. It's a dinosaur egg. Soon, a baby dinosaur will hatch from it.
Sally: Really? Do all dinosaurs hatch from eggs?
Dr. Smith: Yes, they do. Oh my! Did you hear that roar?
Tim: Why are the animals running away? They look very scared.
Dr. Smith: That is a Tyrannosaurus.
Tim: It looks dangerous.
Dr. Smith: It is. It's a meat eater.
Tim: What does that mean?
Sally: It means we should run.
Dr. Smith: That's right! Run, Tim! Run, Sally! Let's get out of here. Here's the time machine. Hop in! Come on, we have to be quick.
Sally: Oh no! Here comes the Tyrannosaurus.
Tim: Hurry, hurry, hurry!
Dr. Smith: Now, where is the "present" button?
Sally: Hurry!
Dr. Smith: I found it. Whew! Soon we will be back in the present, safe and sound.
Tim: That was fun! Dr. Smith, what happened to the dinosaurs?
Dr. Smith: They became extinct, Tim.
Sally: Really! How did that happen?
Dr. Smith: Some people think that a very large rock crashed into Earth. There was a lot of smoke and dust, and then the sun went away.
Tim: Without the sun, all the dinosaurs died?
Dr. Smith: Right.
Sally: Dr. Smith, we have to go. Our mother said to be home by five.
Dr. Smith: You had better go quickly.
Tim: Thank you, Dr. Smith. Good-bye!
Dr. Smith: Good-bye.
One day a young bird was learning to fly. "Whee! This is fun!" he said, flapping his wings. Suddenly another bird flew by. "Wow! What kind of bird was that?" he wondered. "How cool!"
He decided to follow the other bird. On his way he met a squirrel. "Hey, Squirrel," he said, "did you see a bird go by?"
The squirrel was confused. "What bird?" he said.
"Just a moment ago, a bird flew by us. Didn’t you see it?" the bird asked again.
The squirrel smiled. "Oh, that was not a bird. That was me!"
"You?" said the bird. "But you are a squirrel! Squirrels cannot fly!"
"Well, I can," said the squirrel. "I am a flying squirrel! Watch me!" The squirrel jumped off the branch. He stretched his arms and legs, and soared through the air.
"Oh, that was awesome!" the little bird said. "But your wings do not look like my wings."
"No," explained the flying squirrel. "I do not have wings. I have flaps of skin on my sides. I stretch these flaps and I can glide for a long time. Now you know flying is not just for birds!"
Just then an insect flew by.
"Oh, my favorite kind of insect!" said the bird.
"Oh, that is my favorite too!" the squirrel agreed.
The squirrel and the bird followed the insect to the stream. Suddenly a fish flew out of the water and glided by them.
"What was that? Did you see it?" asked the squirrel.
"I cannot believe what I saw!" said the bird. "Fish cannot fly!"

The fish swam up to them. "You are right!" the fish said. "But I can. I am a flying fish. "I can glide through the air when a bigger fish tries to eat me. I have to go now. Bye!" And the fish swam away.
"Gee! I have never seen a fish fly before," said the bird. "Well, Squirrel, you were right! I guess flying really isn’t just for birds."
"Good-bye, Bird," said the squirrel. "I have to tell my family about the flying fish!" He leaped into the air.
"Good-bye!" said the bird. "I have to tell my mom about this. You never know what might fly by!"

15.title: How Animals Survive in the Desert

paragraphs.text: Sparrow: Whew! It is so hot here! I have been flying over this desert all day. I need to find a cool place to rest. Look, there's a hole in the ground. I'll rest there.
Mouse: Who are you?
Sparrow: Oh, I'm sorry. I am a sparrow. This desert is so dry and hot that I did not expect to see any animals living here!
Mouse: I am a desert mouse, and there are a lot of animals here.
Sparrow: Really?
Mouse: Yes. The days are very hot and dry, but the nights are cold. So most desert animals do not move around during the day.
Sparrow: But how do they endure so much heat? It is so hot that I am about to die!

Mouse: Well, some desert animals use parts of their bodies to cool off. For example, desert owls open their mouths wide and flutter their throats. The jackrabbit's ears are long and have many blood vessels. The heat is released through the blood vessels in its long ears.
Sparrow: Oh, that's interesting! Up north, I have seen other rabbits, and their ears are much shorter.

Mouse: Yes, up north, they do not need long ears to survive. All over the world, animals are suited to their different habitats. For example, most desert animals are light-colored. Their lighter colors keep them from getting really hot too.
Sparrow: Then what about the darker animals? They would get much hotter than light-colored animals. Right?
Mouse: You are right. Vultures are dark-colored, but they wet their legs with their urine. The urine cools the blood in their legs. The cooler blood goes back through their bodies.
Sparrow: I see. They are really amazing! Then how do desert animals find water? You do need water, don't you?
Mouse: Of course! We desert creatures get water from plants. The juicy cactus is a favorite! Have a piece!
Sparrow: But won't I get stuck by the thorns?
Mouse: Not really. Go ahead, just be careful.
Sparrow: Hmm, not bad! By the way, how do you stay cool in this desert?
Mouse: I live in an underground den like this. I close the opening when it is very hot. That keeps out the heat. Then I can save the moisture from my breath.
Sparrow: Wonderful! Desert animals are really amazing. But I might not survive here.

Mouse: That's true. The desert gets very little rain. It gets less than 25 centimeters of rain a year! So all the animals in the desert have special ways to help them survive. But you have wings. You can fly to a place where you will survive well.
Sparrow: Yes, you are right! I have to leave now. Thank you for telling me about desert animals. Good-bye!
Mouse: My pleasure! Good-bye!
Have you seen these seabirds before? They are emperor penguins. They look very dressed up, don't they?
These emperor penguins are playing and catching fish in the ocean. But what do they do when the wind gets colder?
"Brr! Winter must be around the corner!" says one emperor penguin.
"Yes, it is time to lay our egg," says the other.
"Oh, I can't wait to be a father!"
So the two emperor penguins swim to the frozen shore of Antarctica. The weather is bitterly cold. The father finds shelter under an ice cliff. Then the mother emperor penguin lays her egg.

"Dear, you did such a good job! Look at our beautiful egg! Quick, roll it onto my feet so I can keep it warm." The father emperor penguin carefully balances the egg on his feet. He makes sure the egg doesn't touch the ice. To keep the egg warm, he covers it with the extra skin over his stomach.
"Now head out to sea to eat and rest. You worked very hard," says the father.
"I am very tired," says the mother penguin. "But I can stay on shore. I want to stay with you and our egg."
But the father emperor penguin insists. "No, you go and rest. I will take care of our egg until you come back."
"Okay, dear, I guess I will. Please stay warm and keep our egg safe!"

After the mother penguin leaves, it gets colder and colder. The father emperor penguin and his friends huddle together to keep warm. They cannot leave their eggs to hunt or fish. They must sit on their eggs for nine long weeks.
"Brr! Hey, are you guys okay?"
"Brr! Yes, I am doing fine. But it is pretty cold, isn't it?"
"Yep! And we have many more weeks to go. Brr!"
"I am getting so hungry!" thinks the father emperor penguin. "But it's my job to guard the egg and keep it warm. I hope it survives the harsh winter."
Finally the egg begins to hatch.
"Cheep, cheep!" A fuzzy, gray emperor penguin peeps up at its father.
"Look at my beautiful baby! I am so proud!"

When the mother returns, she says, "Oh, how wonderful! Look at my fuzzy little chick! Thank you, dear. Now I am strong and rested again. But look how thin you are. You have not eaten for over nine weeks. Let's take turns. Now I can take care of our baby. You must eat and rest. Our baby will need a strong father to protect him."
"You are right. I will be back soon." So the father emperor penguin heads to the ocean. While he is gone, the mother feeds and cares for the chick.
Soon the father emperor penguin returns.
"Are you strong and rested?" asks the mother emperor penguin.
"Yes, I feel so much better now. Look what I brought you both from the ocean!"
"A squid! My favorite!"
"Cheep, cheep!" says the baby. It's his favorite too.
The emperor penguins look so happy together! Isn't the emperor penguin family great?
